Neutrino oscillation is a quantum mechanical phenomenon where a neutrino created with a specific lepton flavour (
u_e, 
u_\mu, 
u_	au) is later measured to have a different flavour[cite: 1]. Experiments probe these quantum transitions using two primary, complementary measurement strategies. Appearance searches look for a specific neutrino flavour in the detector that was not present in the initial beam or source, such as detecting 
u_e from an initial 
u_\mu beam[cite: 1]. These offer exceptional sensitivity to small mixing angles and CP-violating phases because background levels from intrinsic flavour contamination are generally low[cite: 1]. Conversely, disappearance searches measure the survival probability of the initial neutrino flavour, such as tracking  ar{
u}_e 	o  ar{
u}_e or 
u_\mu 	o 
u_\mu[cite: 1]. By mapping the deficit in expected flux as a function of energy and baseline distance, disappearance channels provide direct, high-precision constraints on mass-squared splittings and mixing angles[cite: 1].

To probe these oscillations across vastly different baselines (L) and energies (E), experimentalists utilize diverse terrestrial and natural neutrino sources[cite: 1]. Accelerator neutrinos are produced artificially by colliding high-energy protons into heavy targets like graphite or beryllium to generate pions and kaons, which subsequently decay into directed, high-purity beams of 
u_\mu or  ar{
u}_\mu in the MeV to GeV energy range[cite: 1]. Reactor neutrinos serve as intense, terrestrial sources of pure electron antineutrinos ( ar{
u}_e) emitted isotropically via nuclear fission of ^{235}	ext{U}, ^{238}	ext{U}, ^{239}	ext{Pu}, and ^{241}	ext{Pu} at low energy scales between 1	ext{ MeV} and 8	ext{ MeV}[cite: 1].

Natural sources provide complementary energy regimes and baselines[cite: 1]. Solar neutrinos are low-energy 
u_e (< 20	ext{ MeV}) produced via nuclear fusion chains in the Sun’s core, providing essential insights into matter-enhanced oscillation mechanisms known as the MSW effect[cite: 1]. Atmospheric neutrinos span a broad energy range from MeV to TeV scales and are generated when high-energy cosmic rays strike Earth’s upper atmosphere, producing hadronic showers that decay into 
u_e and 
u_\mu with baselines ranging from 10	ext{ km} overhead to 13,000	ext{ km} through the Earth’s core[cite: 1]. Finally, astrophysical sources yield extreme fluxes: cosmogenic neutrinos are produced at ultra-high energies (PeV to EeV) when cosmic rays interact with the Cosmic Microwave Background via the GZK effect, while extragalactic neutrinos (TeV to PeV) originate from high-energy cosmic accelerators such as Active Galactic Nuclei, blazars, and Gamma-Ray Bursts beyond the Milky Way[cite: 1].

The following sections summarize the current, legacy, and next-generation suite of neutrino oscillation experiments globally, categorized by primary source and baseline[cite: 1].

Location: Japan (Beam: J-PARC in Tokai; Far Detector: Kamioka Observatory, Gifu)

Baseline (L): 295\text{ km} (Far Detector); 280\text{ m} (Near Detector ND280)

Detector Technology:

Near Detectors (ND280, INGRID): Plastic scintillators, TPCs, and fine-grained detectors inside a magnet.

Far Detector (Super-Kamiokande): A 50 kt water Cherenkov detector viewed by over 11,000 PMTs.

Timeline: Started 2010; currently running (Phase-II upgrades ongoing).

Neutrino Source: Accelerator (an off-axis 1.6^\circ narrow-band \nu_\mu / \bar{\nu}_\mu beam generated by 30 GeV protons hitting a graphite target).

Primary Flavour: \nu_\mu / \bar{\nu}_\mu

Energy Range: Peak energy E_\nu \sim 0.6\text{ GeV}

Primary Oscillation Parameters: Mixing angle \theta_{23}, mass-squared difference |\Delta m^2_{32}|, and the CP-violating phase \delta_{\text{CP}}.

Dominant Systematics & Backgrounds:

Systematics: Complex neutrino-nucleus interaction modelling (such as multinucleon 2p2h processes) and flux normalization.

Backgrounds: Neutral current events with a single pion (\text{NC}1\pi^0) where photon showers mimic single electron tracks from \nu_e interactions.

Secondary Physics Goals: Neutrino-nucleus cross-section measurements, sterile neutrino searches, and non-standard interactions.

Fun Fact: The beamline targets a massive underground water tank situated 295 km away. To line up the beam with pinpoint accuracy, geodetic survey techniques were refined using GPS and satellite data, pointing the beam directly through the Earth’s crust so that it grazes the detector underground![cite: 1]

Location: United States (Beam/Near Detector: Fermilab, Batavia, IL; Far Detector: Ash River, MN)

Baseline (L): 810\text{ km} (Far Detector); 1\text{ km} (Near Detector)

Detector Technology: Extruded PVC cells filled with liquid scintillator, read out using wavelength-shifting fibres connected to Avalanche Photodiodes (APDs).

Timeline: Started 2014; currently running.

Neutrino Source: Accelerator (NuMI off-axis 14\text{ mrad} beam produced by 120 GeV protons from the Main Injector).

Primary Flavour: \nu_\mu / \bar{\nu}_\mu

Energy Range: Peak energy E_\nu \sim 2.0\text{ GeV}

Primary Oscillation Parameters: Mass Ordering (Normal vs. Inverted via Earth matter effects), \theta_{23} octant, and \delta_{\text{CP}}.

Dominant Systematics & Backgrounds:

Systematics: Absolute light level calibration, detector energy scale, and cross-section modelling.

Backgrounds: Unshielded cosmic-ray muons (due to the detector’s location on the surface), intrinsic beam \nu_e, and neutral current events producing neutral pions.

Secondary Physics Goals: Core-collapse supernova neutrino detection, atmospheric neutrino monitoring, cosmic-ray physics, and searches for magnetic monopoles.

Fun Fact: Because the Far Detector sits on the surface without the shielding of a deep cave, it gets blasted by roughly 150,000 cosmic rays per second. To spot a handful of neutrino interactions a day amidst that noise, the detector uses ultra-precise timing synchronization down to nanoseconds![cite: 1]

Location: United States (Beam/Near Detector: Fermilab, IL; Far Detector: SURF, Lead, SD)

Baseline (L): 1,300\text{ km} (Far Detector); 574\text{ m} (Near Detector)

Detector Technology:

Near Detector: Multi-component system (Liquid Argon TPC, SAND detector, and mobile ND-GAr).

Far Detector: Four 17 kt modules using Liquid Argon Time Projection Chamber (LArTPC) technology, located 1,480 m underground.

Timeline: Construction ongoing; first data expected in the late 2020s.

Neutrino Source: Accelerator (LBNF broadband beam generated by 60–120 GeV protons).

Primary Flavour: \nu_\mu / \bar{\nu}_\mu

Energy Range: Broadband 0.5\text{ GeV} - 5.0\text{ GeV}

Primary Oscillation Parameters: Unambiguous discovery of CP violation (\delta_{\text{CP}}) across a broad spectrum, Mass Ordering (>5\sigma), \theta_{23}, and \Delta m^2_{31}.

Dominant Systematics & Backgrounds:

Systematics: LArTPC absolute energy scale calibration, shower reconstruction efficiency, and Final State Interactions (FSI) inside the argon nucleus.

Backgrounds: Intrinsic beam \nu_e contamination and misidentified neutral current events with high-momentum neutral pions.

Secondary Physics Goals: Searches for proton decay (specifically \text{p} \to \text{K}^+ \bar{\nu}), core-collapse supernova electron-neutrino bursts, and BSM physics (e.g., light dark matter, heavy neutral leptons).

Fun Fact: The Far Detector is taking over the historic underground cavity where Ray Davis conducted his Nobel Prize-winning Homestake solar neutrino experiment in the late 1960s—where the original “Solar Neutrino Problem” was born![cite: 1]

Location: United States (Fermilab, Batavia, IL)

Baseline (L): 110\text{ m} (SBND), 470\text{ m} (MicroBooNE), 600\text{ m} (ICARUS)

Detector Technology: Liquid Argon Time Projection Chambers (LArTPCs). The SBN program comprises three detectors along the same beamline:

SBND (Near Detector, 110 m): 112-ton active LArTPC.

MicroBooNE (Intermediate, 470 m): 85-ton active LArTPC.

ICARUS (Far Detector, 600 m): 476-ton active LArTPC (relocated from LNGS, Italy).

Timeline: MicroBooNE ran 2015–2021; ICARUS began taking data in 2021; SBND began physics data collection in late 2024. Program currently running.

Neutrino Source: Accelerator (Booster Neutrino Beam [BNB] generated by 8 GeV protons hitting a beryllium target).

Primary Flavour: \nu_\mu (with search for \nu_e appearance and \nu_\mu disappearance)

Energy Range: Peak energy E_\nu \sim 0.7\text{ GeV} - 0.8\text{ GeV}

Primary Oscillation Parameters: Short-baseline oscillations driven by an eV-scale mass splitting (\Delta m^2_{41} \sim 1\text{ eV}^2), searching for sterile neutrino mixing (\theta_{14}, \theta_{24}).

Dominant Systematics & Backgrounds:

Systematics: Flux shape uncertainties, electron-photon discrimination in LAr, and low-energy neutrino-argon interaction cross sections.

Backgrounds: Single-photon shower events (\text{NC}\Delta \to N\gamma), intrinsic beam \nu_e, and cosmic rays entering the shallow surface-level detectors.

Secondary Physics Goals: High-statistics measurement of low-energy neutrino-argon cross sections, Dark Sector particle searches (light dark matter, heavy neutral leptons), and detector technology validation for DUNE.

Fun Fact: The SBND oscillation working group and detector development involve major key contributions from researchers at the University of Sheffield![cite: 1]

Location: United States (Fermilab, Batavia, IL)

Baseline (L): 541\text{ m}

Detector Technology: 800-ton pure mineral oil Cherenkov detector equipped with 1,280 PMTs.

Timeline: 2002 – 2019 (Completed).

Neutrino Source: Accelerator (Booster Neutrino Beam at 541 m baseline).

Primary Flavour: \nu_\mu / \bar{\nu}_\mu

Energy Range: 0.2\text{ GeV} - 1.25\text{ GeV}

Primary Oscillation Parameters: Short-baseline \nu_\mu \to \nu_e appearance (\Delta m^2 \sim 0.1 - 10\text{ eV}^2).

Dominant Systematics & Backgrounds:

Systematics: Beam flux predictions and misidentified neutral-current pion production.

Backgrounds: Neutral-current \pi^0 events where one photon was lost, mimicking electron Cherenkov rings.

Secondary Physics Goals: Cross-section measurements on carbon targets, dark matter searches in beam-dump mode.

Fun Fact: MiniBooNE ran for nearly two decades and accumulated a massive, puzzling 4.8\sigma excess of electron-like events that confounded theorists for years, driving the development of the entire modern short-baseline liquid argon research program![cite: 1]

Location: China (Daya Bay/Ling Ao Nuclear Power Plant, Shenzhen)

Baseline (L): 360\text{ m} - 500\text{ m} (Near Hall detectors); 1.5\text{ km} - 1.9\text{ km} (Far Hall detectors)

Detector Technology: Gadolinium-doped Liquid Scintillator (Gd-LS) nested in an un-doped LS buffer inside PMT-instrumented tanks submerged in water pools.

Timeline: 2011 – 2020 (Completed).

Neutrino Source: Commercial nuclear reactors (6 \times 2.9\text{ GW}_{\text{th}} cores).

Primary Flavour: Electron antineutrinos (\bar{\nu}_e)

Energy Range: 1.0\text{ MeV} - 8.0\text{ MeV}

Primary Oscillation Parameters: Precision measurement of mixing angle \theta_{13} and effective mass-squared splitting |\Delta m^2_{ee}|.

Dominant Systematics & Backgrounds:

Systematics: Target mass uncertainty across identical modules and reactor flux model uncertainties (including the infamous “5 MeV bump”).

Backgrounds: Cosmogenic isotopes (^9\text{Li}/^8\text{He}) and fast neutrons from cosmic-ray spallation.

Secondary Physics Goals: Precision reactor antineutrino spectrum and flux mapping, light sterile neutrino searches (4th mass state).

Fun Fact: The experiment was a literal race against time. Daya Bay was built to catch the then-unknown mixing angle \theta_{13}. They announced a non-zero measurement in 2012 with 5.2\sigma significance, beating international competitors to the punch and revealing that \theta_{13} was surprisingly large![cite: 1]

Location: China (Kaiping, Jiangmen, Guangdong)

Baseline (L): 52.5\text{ km} (equalized baseline to both the Yangjiang and Taishan Nuclear Power Plants)

Detector Technology: A 20 kt liquid scintillator sphere enclosed in a giant 35.4 m acrylic vessel, monitored by over 20,000 20-inch PMTs inside a 44 m water pool.

Timeline: Began collecting data in August 2025; currently running.

Neutrino Source: Yangjiang and Taishan Nuclear Power Plants (at an optimized 53 km baseline).

Primary Flavour: Electron antineutrinos (\bar{\nu}_e)

Energy Range: 1.0\text{ MeV} - 8.0\text{ MeV}

Primary Oscillation Parameters: Mass Ordering via sub-percent energy resolution (\le 3\% \text{ at } 1\text{ MeV}), and ultra-precise measurement of \sin^2\theta_{12}, \Delta m^2_{21}, and |\Delta m^2_{32}|.

Dominant Systematics & Backgrounds:

Systematics: Non-linearity of the energy response, optical transparency of the liquid scintillator over long paths, and reactor flux variations.

Backgrounds: Cosmogenic ^9\text{Li}/^8\text{He}, (\alpha, n) radioactive reactions from surrounding material, and background geoneutrinos.

Secondary Physics Goals: Geoneutrinos from Earth’s crust/mantle, Diffuse Supernova Neutrino Background (DSNB), solar neutrinos, and atmospheric neutrinos.

Fun Fact: The central sphere holds 20,000 tons of liquid scintillator inside an acrylic shell just 12 cm thick—making it the largest single acrylic structure ever built in human history![cite: 1]

Location: Japan (Kamioka Observatory, Hida, Gifu)

Baseline (L): Solar: 1.5 \times 10^8\text{ km}; Atmospheric: 10\text{ km} - 13,000\text{ km} (variable path length through Earth)

Detector Technology: 50 kt ultra-pure water Cherenkov detector (currently in the SK-Gd phase with dissolved Gadolinium sulphate).

Timeline: Started 1996; currently running.

Neutrino Source: Cosmic rays interacting in the atmosphere, and solar fusion reactions (^8\text{B}, \text{hep}).

Primary Flavour: \nu_e, \bar{\nu}_e, \nu_\mu, \bar{\nu}_\mu

Energy Range: Solar: 3.5\text{ MeV} - 20\text{ MeV}; Atmospheric: 100\text{ MeV} to TeV scale

Primary Oscillation Parameters: Atmospheric \theta_{23} and |\Delta m^2_{32}|, solar \theta_{12} and \Delta m^2_{21} (via day/night matter effects).

Dominant Systematics & Backgrounds:

Systematics: 3D atmospheric flux modelling uncertainties and primary hadron interaction models.

Backgrounds: Radon (^{222}\text{Rn}) decays in water at low energies, and neutral current atmospheric interactions.

Secondary Physics Goals: Proton decay searches (\text{p} \to e^+ \pi^0), galactic core-collapse supernova warnings, DSNB, and dark matter searches.

Fun Fact: The water inside Super-K is so ultra-pure that it acts as a harsh solvent; it can slowly leach ions out of normal metals and plastics, and scientists must navigate the tank in rubber dinghies during rare maintenance periods to keep from contaminating it![cite: 1]

Location: Japan (Kamioka, Hida, Gifu; J-PARC beamline from Tokai)

Baseline (L): Accelerator Beam: 295\text{ km}; Solar: 1.5 \times 10^8\text{ km}; Atmospheric: 10\text{ km} - 13,000\text{ km}

Detector Technology: Next-generation subterranean water Cherenkov detector containing 258 kt of ultra-pure water (190 kt fiducial mass)—over 8 times the fiducial volume of Super-Kamiokande—instrumented with ultra-high-sensitivity PMTs.

Timeline: Construction ongoing; planned operations start in late 2027 or 2028.

Neutrino Source: Upgraded high-intensity J-PARC accelerator narrow-band beam (1.3\text{ MW} proton beam), along with atmospheric and solar neutrinos.

Primary Flavour: \nu_\mu, \bar{\nu}_\mu, \nu_e, \bar{\nu}_e

Energy Range: Solar: >2\text{ MeV}; Beam/Atmospheric: 100\text{ MeV} - \text{tens of GeV}

Primary Oscillation Parameters: High-precision determination of leptonic CP violation (\delta_{\text{CP}}) covering over 60\% of parameter space at >5\sigma, precise mixing angle \theta_{23} octant, and mass squared differences.

Dominant Systematics & Backgrounds:

Systematics: Neutrino interaction cross-section models, beam flux uncertainties, and PMT timing/photosensor calibration.

Backgrounds: Atmospheric \text{NC}1\pi^0 interactions mimicking \nu_e single-ring events, and cosmic-ray spallation products.

Secondary Physics Goals: Unprecedented sensitivity to proton decay (\text{p} \to e^+ \pi^0 lifetime sensitivity exceeding 

1035 years), galactic supernova burst detection (expecting tens of thousands of events within seconds), solar neutrino day-night asymmetry, and DSNB discovery.

Fun Fact: Hyper-K’s main underground cavern is so colossal (60 metres in diameter and 71 metres tall) that it could easily fit the entire United States Capitol building inside it![cite: 1]

Location: Amundsen-Scott South Pole Station, Antarctica

Baseline (L): Atmospheric: 20\text{ km} - 12,700\text{ km} (depending on zenith angle through Earth); Astrophysical: > 10^{19}\text{ km}

Detector Technology: A 1\text{ km}^3 array of Digital Optical Modules (DOMs) melted deep into the Antarctic ice cap; DeepCore is a densely instrumented sub-array at its center.

Timeline: Started 2010; currently running.

Neutrino Source: High-energy atmospheric cosmic ray air showers.

Primary Flavour: \nu_\mu, \bar{\nu}_\mu, \nu_e, \bar{\nu}_e, \nu_\tau, \bar{\nu}_\tau

Energy Range: DeepCore: 5\text{ GeV} - 100\text{ GeV}; IceCube Main Array: >100\text{ GeV} to PeV scale

Primary Oscillation Parameters: Atmospheric mixing parameters \theta_{23} and |\Delta m^2_{32}|, and tau neutrino (\nu_\tau) appearance.

Dominant Systematics & Backgrounds:

Systematics: Optical properties of deep glacial ice (light scattering, absorption, and directional anisotropy caused by dust layers from prehistoric volcanic eruptions), and DOM angular sensitivity.

Backgrounds: Downward-going cosmic-ray atmospheric muons.

Secondary Physics Goals: High-energy neutrino astrophysics (blazars, GRBs), cosmic-ray anisotropy, and searches for sterile neutrinos.

Fun Fact: To install the optical sensors, engineers used a hot-water drill system that carved out 2.5 km deep, 60 cm wide holes into the Antarctic ice sheet in under two days per hole, stringing up PMTs before the holes froze back solid![cite: 1]

The Standard Model of particle physics classifies all known fundamental particles into elementary matter particles (fermions) and force-carrying particles (bosons).

Fermions are divided into two distinct families:

Quarks: Particles that interact via the strong force (as well as weak and electromagnetic forces) to form hadrons like protons and neutrons.

Leptons: Particles that do not feel the strong nuclear force.

Leptons are split into two categories:

Charged Leptons: The electron (e^-), muon (\mu^-), and tau (\tau^-), which carry an electric charge of -1e and interact via electromagnetism and the weak force.

Neutral Leptons (Neutrinos): The electron neutrino (\nu_e), muon neutrino (\nu_\mu), and tau neutrino (\nu_\tau), which carry zero electric charge and interact only via the weak nuclear force (and gravity).

Because neutrinos lack electric charge and colour charge, they pass through ordinary matter almost unimpeded. In the original Standard Model framework, neutrinos were assumed to be massless, left-handed particles.

In the early 20th century, measurements of beta decay showed that electrons were emitted with a continuous spectrum of energies, appearing to violate the laws of conservation of energy and momentum.

1930 (The Hypothesis): Wolfgang Pauli proposed a neutral, lightweight particle—the “neutrino”—emitted alongside the electron during beta decay to carry away the missing energy and momentum.

1956 (Discovery): Clyde Cowan and Frederick Reines experimentally detected electron antineutrinos near a nuclear reactor via inverse beta decay.

1960s (The Solar Neutrino Problem): Raymond Davis Jr. built a massive underground detector filled with cleaning fluid (tetrachloroethylene) in the Homestake Gold Mine. He measured the flux of electron neutrinos coming from nuclear fusion in the centre of the Sun but consistently detected only about one-third to one-half of the rate predicted by astrophysicist John Bahcall’s solar models.

1998–2001 (Resolution): The Super-Kamiokande experiment in Japan (studying atmospheric neutrinos) and the Sudbury Neutrino Observatory (SNO) in Canada (studying solar neutrinos) confirmed that neutrinos change “flavour” on their way to Earth. This phenomenon is known as neutrino oscillation.

Neutrinos come in three distinct flavours associated with their corresponding charged leptons:

Electron neutrino (\nu_e)

Muon neutrino (\nu_\mu)

Tau neutrino (\nu_\tau)

The key to neutrino oscillations lies in the distinction between how neutrinos interact and how they travel:

Flavour Eigenstates (\nu_e, \nu_\mu, \nu_\tau): States produced or detected in weak interactions alongside an electron, muon, or tau.

Mass Eigenstates (\nu_1, \nu_2, \nu_3): States with definite, specific masses (m_1, m_2, m_3) that propagate through space as matter waves.

A neutrino produced as a specific flavour is not a single particle with a single mass, but rather a quantum superposition (a linear combination) of mass states.

When an electron neutrino (
u_e) is created, it is emitted as a wave packet made of 
u_1, 
u_2, and 
u_3.

As the neutrino travels through space at near light speed, the mass components travel with slightly different wave frequencies because their masses (m_1, m_2, m_3) differ.

This difference in propagation speeds creates an interference pattern (similar to musical “beats”).

As a result, the probability of detecting the particle as a 
u_e, 
u_\mu, or 
u_	au oscillates as a function of distance travelled.

For simplified calculations involving two-neutrino mixing, the probability (P) that a neutrino of flavour \alpha transforms into flavour \beta after travelling a distance L with energy E is:P(\nu_\alpha \rightarrow \nu_\beta) = \sin^2(2\theta) \cdot \sin^2\left( \frac{\Delta m^2 \cdot L}{4E} \right)

In the general three-flavour framework, the transition probability from initial flavour \alpha to final flavour \beta includes both CP-conserving (real) and CP-violating (imaginary) components:P(\nu_\alpha \rightarrow \nu_\beta) = \delta_{\alpha\beta} - 4 \sum_{i > j} \text{Re}(U_{\alpha i}^* U_{\beta i} U_{\alpha j} U_{\beta j}^*) \sin^2\left( \frac{\Delta m_{ij}^2 \cdot L}{4E} \right) + 2 \sum_{i > j} \text{Im}(U_{\alpha i}^* U_{\beta i} U_{\alpha j} U_{\beta j}^*) \sin\left( \frac{\Delta m_{ij}^2 \cdot L}{2E} \right)

Where:

\delta_{\alpha\beta}: Kronecker delta (1 if \alpha = \beta, 0 if \alpha \neq \beta).

U_{\alpha i}: Elements of the PMNS matrix.

\text{Re}(\dots) & \text{Im}(\dots): The real and imaginary parts of the PMNS matrix element product.

\Delta m_{ij}^2 = m_i^2 - m_j^2: Mass-squared differences between mass states i and j.

L: Distance travelled from source to detector.

E: Energy of the neutrino.

(Note: For antineutrinos, the sign of the imaginary term is reversed, allowing tests for CP violation.)

records.content: While the standard 3-flavour oscillation framework successfully explains the majority of solar, atmospheric, and long-baseline reactor data, several persistent experimental anomalies at short baselines (where L/E \sim 1\text{ m/MeV} or 1\text{ km/GeV}) conflict with standard predictions.

LSND and MiniBooNE Anomalies: The Liquid Scintillator Neutrino Detector (LSND) and MiniBooNE experiments observed a significant excess of electron-type (anti)neutrinos in muon (anti)neutrino beams over short distances. This suggested an oscillation driven by a mass-squared difference of \Delta m^2 \sim 1\text{ eV}^2—much larger than the solar (\sim 10^{-5}\text{ eV}^2) or atmospheric (\sim 10^{-3}\text{ eV}^2) mass splittings.

Gallium Anomaly: Underground calibration tests using radioactive sources (SAGE, GALLEX, and BEST) measured an unexpected deficit (20–24%) of electron neutrinos reacting with gallium targets at distances of less than a few metres.

Reactor Antineutrino Anomaly: Early re-evaluations of reactor fluxes indicated an overall deficit in expected electron antineutrinos detected a short distance from nuclear cores.

Recent high-precision measurements have severely constrained the simplest “3+1” single sterile neutrino scenario:

High-precision experiments like MicroBooNE at Fermilab and KATRIN tritium decay measurements have strongly disfavoured or ruled out the baseline “3+1” model across significant portions of its expected parameter space.

Alternative BSM solutions under active investigation include:

Multi-Sterile Models (3+N): Incorporating two or more sterile states to account for complex interference patterns.

Decaying Sterile Neutrinos: Models where a heavy sterile state decays in flight into lighter particles (e.g., a photon or scalar boson plus an active neutrino), producing the observed excess electromagnetic signals.

Non-Standard Interactions (NSIs): Hypothesising new, exotic fundamental forces or matter interactions that modify neutrino propagation without needing additional physical mass states.

records.content:
According to the Big Bang model, equal amounts of matter and antimatter should have been created in the early universe. Had they behaved identically, they would have completely annihilated, leaving behind a universe made purely of photons.

To explain why our universe is made almost entirely of matter, Andrei Sakharov showed that three conditions must be met:

Baryon number violation: Mechanisms that change the net amount of matter.

(C) and CP violation: Differences in physical behaviour between matter and antimatter.

Interactions out of thermal equilibrium: Processes occurring during rapid cosmic expansion.

While CP violation is observed in the quark sector, it is mathematically far too small to explain the observed surplus of matter.

Leptogenesis is a primary BSM candidate for solving this puzzle using neutrino CP violation:

Heavy Majorana Neutrinos: Very heavy, right-handed neutrinos created at extremely high energies in the early universe decay unevenly into leptons versus antileptons due to leptonic CP violation (\delta \neq 0).

Lepton-to-Baryon Conversion: Sphaleron processes (non-perturbative electroweak interactions) then convert this excess of leptons into a net surplus of baryons (protons and neutrons).

Thus, measuring CP violation in current and upcoming long-baseline experiments (such as DUNE and Hyper-Kamiokande) could provide the crucial evidence explaining why matter exists today.

Non-Zero Mass: If neutrino oscillations occur, then at least two \Delta m^2 values must be non-zero, mathematically proving that neutrinos must have non-zero mass.

Standard Model Extension: The original Standard Model assumed neutrinos were completely massless. The discovery of oscillations required a fundamental expansion of particle physics theory, and ongoing short-baseline anomalies continue to push searches for new physics.

Cosmological Link: Leptonic CP violation via neutrino oscillations offers one of the most promising avenues to explain the matter-antimatter asymmetry of the Universe.

Statistical Methods for Neutrino Oscillation Parameter Estimation & Contour Generation

records.content:
As established previously, in a simplified two-flavour approximation, the probability that a neutrino of initial flavour \alpha is detected as flavour \beta after travelling a distance L (in km) with energy E (in GeV) is given by:P_{\alpha \to \beta}(E, L; \mathbf{\psi}) = \sin^2(2\theta) \sin^2\left( 1.27 \, \frac{\Delta m^2 \, [\text{eV}^2] \, L \, [\text{km}]}{E \, [\text{GeV}]} \right)

where \mathbf{\psi} = (\theta, \Delta m^2) represents the vector of physical oscillation parameters.

Experimentally, neutrino detectors do not measure the continuous probability function directly, nor do they measure the true incoming neutrino energy E (often denoted E_{\text{true}}) with perfect accuracy. Instead, detectors measure final-state particle tracks and energy deposits to compute a reconstructed energy, E_{\text{rec}}.

The reconstructed energy E_{\text{rec}} is a smeared observation of E_{\text{true}}, governed by the detector’s energy resolution, thresholds, and missing neutral energy (e.g., escaping neutrons). This relationship is formally bridged by the response matrix R(E_{\text{rec}}, E_{\text{true}}), which defines the conditional probability density of observing E_{\text{rec}} given a true incoming energy E_{\text{true}}.

Neutrino oscillation parameter estimation relies on observing how the binned histogram of reconstructed energy E_{\text{rec}} is modulated relative to the unoscillated prediction:

Disappearance Mode (e.g., \nu_\mu \to \nu_\mu): The oscillation manifests as a characteristic “dip” or deficit in the event count histogram around the reconstructed energy corresponding to maximum oscillation probability (where 1.27 \Delta m^2 L / E_{\text{true}} \approx \pi / 2). The depth of this dip constrains the mixing angle \sin^2(2\theta), while the energy position of the minimum constrains the mass-squared difference \Delta m^2.

Appearance Mode (e.g., \nu_\mu \to \nu_e): The signal appears as an excess of events above background in a channel that was originally absent or suppressed in the initial flux.

Near-to-Far Baseline Ratios: Long-baseline experiments frequently deploy two detectors: a Near Detector placed close to the neutrino source (where oscillations have not yet developed) to measure the unoscillated flux and cross-sections, and a Far Detector placed at distance L to record the oscillated spectrum. Comparing event counts bin-by-bin between the Far and Near detectors cancels major correlated systematic uncertainties in the flux and interaction physics.

In an actual experimental detector, the expected number of events \mu_i in reconstructed energy bin i integrates over all true incoming energies E_{\text{true}} weighted by the probability P_{\alpha \to \beta}(E_{\text{true}}, L; \mathbf{\psi}) and smeared by R(E_{\text{rec}}, E_{\text{true}}):\mu_i(\mathbf{\psi}) = \int_{\text{bin } i} dE_{\text{rec}} \int dE_{\text{true}} \, \Phi(E_{\text{true}}) \, P_{\alpha \to \beta}(E_{\text{true}}, L; \mathbf{\psi}) \, \sigma(E_{\text{true}}) \, R(E_{\text{rec}}, E_{\text{true}}) \, \epsilon(E_{\text{rec}}) + B_i

where \Phi(E_{\text{true}}) is the initial flux, \sigma(E_{\text{true}}) is the interaction cross-section, \epsilon(E_{\text{rec}}) is the detection efficiency, and B_i is the expected background contribution.

records.content:
In a simple physics experiment, you might predict outcome probabilities using a direct formula. However, calculating the expected event count \mu_i(\mathbf{\psi}) analytically is practically impossible. A realistic neutrino experiment involves complex, non-linear cross-sections \sigma(E_{\text{true}}), complicated detector geometry, and intricate energy loss mechanisms as charged particles track through matter.

To overcome this, experimentalists use Monte Carlo (MC) simulations. Named after the famous casino, the Monte Carlo method uses pseudo-random numbers to simulate millions of individual, hypothetical particle interactions one-by-one according to the laws of quantum mechanics and classical physics. By aggregating millions of these simulated events, we build up predicted histograms that can be directly compared with real experimental data.

records.content:
Before a particle enters a detector, its initial interaction must be generated using dedicated event-generation software (such as GENIE or NEUT).

Sampling Neutrino Energy: The initial flux \Phi(E_{\text{true}}) gives a continuous probability distribution of incoming energies. The simulator uses random sampling techniques (like rejection sampling) to pick a specific energy E_{\text{true}} for individual simulated event k.

Applying Conservation Laws: When the simulated neutrino strikes an atomic nucleus (e.g., carbon or oxygen in a water or liquid argon target), quantum mechanics dictates the target collision outcome. The generator calculates the probability of producing specific outgoing particles (such as muons, pions, or protons) using interaction cross-sections \sigma(E_{\text{true}}).

Determining Vectors: Using standard relativistic momentum and energy conservation (\sum E_{\text{initial}} = \sum E_{\text{final}} and \sum \mathbf{p}_{\text{initial}} = \sum \mathbf{p}_{\text{final}}), the simulator calculates the initial direction vectors, velocities, and kinetic energies of all final-state particles emerging from the collision vertex.

records.content:
Once the secondary particles leave the atomic nucleus, they travel through the detector medium. Software toolkits like GEANT4 simulate their transport step-by-step:

Ionisation & Radiation Loss: Charged particles (like muons or electrons) lose kinetic energy as they pass through matter by knocking electrons off surrounding atoms (ionisation) or emitting radiation. GEANT4 steps each particle forward by a small distance \Delta x and subtracts energy using stopping-power equations (e.g., the Bethe-Bloch formula).

Signal Generation: The lost energy is converted into detectable signals based on detector technology—for instance, Cherenkov light cones in water, scintillation photons, or drifted ionisation electrons in high-voltage fields.

Detector Geometry: GEANT4 tracks particles through precise 3D CAD models of the apparatus, accounting for dead regions, structural support walls, and physical boundaries where particles might escape unmeasured.

records.content: The raw, simulated signals (photon hits, wire charges) pass through the exact same reconstruction code used for real experimental data. The algorithms re-cluster light hits and fit tracks to output a final reconstructed energy E_{\text{rec}} for each simulated event.

records.content:
Simulating millions of events through full GEANT4 propagation requires enormous computing power. If we want to test a new trial set of oscillation parameters \mathbf{\psi} = (\sin^2 2\theta, \Delta m^2), running the full GEANT4 simulation from scratch for every iteration would be computationally impossible.

Instead, we generate a single, unoscillated Monte Carlo dataset where every simulated event k starts with an initial baseline weight w_k^{(0)} = 1. When testing a specific oscillation hypothesis \mathbf{\psi}, we simply multiply each event’s weight by its calculated oscillation probability based on its known true energy E_{k, \text{true}} and baseline distance L:w_k(\mathbf{\psi}) = w_k^{(0)} \cdot P_{\alpha \to \beta}(E_{k, \text{true}}, L; \mathbf{\psi})

The total predicted count \mu_i(\mathbf{\psi}) in any reconstructed energy bin i is then obtained by summing the weights of all simulated events that fell into that bin:\mu_i(\mathbf{\psi}) = \sum_{k \in \text{bin } i} w_k(\mathbf{\psi})

This reweighting technique allows fitting routines to scan thousands of physics parameter combinations in seconds.

records.content: Before we can use experimental data to estimate unknown physics parameters (like neutrino mixing angles), we need a rigorous way to compare our observed data against theoretical predictions. Two core concepts form the bedrock of this comparison:

records.content:
Suppose you roll a six-sided die 60 times and roll a “6” 18 times instead of the expected 10 times. Is the die biased, or did you just get lucky? A Goodness-of-Fit (GoF) test answers this question quantitatively.

The Null Hypothesis (H_0): We start with a baseline assumption called the null hypothesis. In particle physics, H_0 is usually the statement: “The Monte Carlo simulation perfectly describes the physical reality, and any observed differences are purely due to random statistical fluctuations.”

The Test Statistic (t): We condense the overall discrepancy between the observed data histogram and the predicted simulation into a single number called a test statistic (often denoted t or \chi^2). A test statistic of t = 0 means absolute identical match, while larger values of t represent increasing disagreement.

Evaluating Discrepancy: Rather than giving a simple “yes” or “no”, a GoF test calculates the mathematical probability of getting a test statistic as large as t (or larger) purely by random chance under H_0. If that probability is extremely small, we reject the model hypothesis H_0.

hierarchy.lvl1: Statistical Methods for Neutrino Oscillation Parameter Estimation & Contour Generation
Statistical Methods for Neutrino Oscillation Parameter Estimation & Contour Generation

records.content:
To interpret whether a test statistic value is “large” or “small”, we must know how many independent ways the data was free to deviate from the model. This is controlled by the degrees of freedom (\text{ndof}).

Think of \text{ndof} like solving a system of simultaneous algebraic equations:

Every independent data bin in your histogram gives you +1 piece of information (an independent observation).

Every parameter you estimate or fit from that same data uses up 1 degree of freedom (reducing flexibility).

Every global constraint you enforce (such as fixing the total number of events to match) also uses up 1 degree of freedom.

Formally, the total degrees of freedom is calculated as:\text{ndof} = k - p - c

where:

k is the total number of independent histogram energy bins.

p is the number of free parameters adjusted during the fit (e.g., fitting both \theta and \Delta m^2 gives p = 2).

c is the number of fixed external constraints applied to the dataset.

Intuitive Example: Imagine drawing a straight line through data points (y = mx + c). You are fitting p = 2 parameters (slope m and intercept c). If you only have k = 2 data points, then \text{ndof} = 2 - 2 = 0. The line will fit the points perfectly regardless of physics, meaning you have zero degrees of freedom left to test whether a straight line was actually a good theoretical model! You need k > 2 points (\text{ndof} > 0) to test the model’s validity.

In neutrino physics, \text{ndof} determines the specific shape of the reference statistical distribution (such as the \chi^2_{\text{ndof}} curve) used to convert a raw test statistic into a meaningful p-value.

records.content: Before attempting to extract neutrino oscillation parameters from a Far Detector, we must verify that our Monte Carlo simulation accurately models the unoscillated particle interactions at the Near Detector or in control samples. If the baseline simulation fails to match unoscillated data, any inferred oscillation signal will be invalid.

records.content:
In an A-level physics lab, when you measure a line of best fit, you calculate deviations using \text{residual} = y_i - y_{\text{model}}. Pearson’s \chi^2 test applies the same logic to histogram bins:\chi^2_{\text{Pearson}} = \sum_{i=1}^k \frac{(N_i - \mu_i)^2}{\mu_i}

Numerator—Square of Deviations: For bin i, we take the difference between observed counts N_i and expected simulation counts \mu_i, then square it (N_i - \mu_i)^2. Squaring ensures that positive and negative discrepancies do not cancel each other out.

Denominator—Variance Weighting: According to Poisson statistics, for a count of \mu_i, the natural statistical variance is \sigma_i^2 = \mu_i. Dividing by \mu_i scales each bin discrepancy by its expected random variance. A discrepancy of 10 events is huge if you only expected 5 (\frac{10^2}{5} = 20), but negligible if you expected 1,000 (\frac{10^2}{1000} = 0.1).

Interpretation: If the simulation is correct, the average contribution from each bin to the sum is roughly 1. Therefore, a good fit yields an overall \chi^2_{\text{Pearson}} \approx \text{ndof}. A ratio \chi^2 / \text{ndof} \gg 1 signals significant data-MC disagreement.

Condition: This approximation assumes Gaussian-like bin fluctuations, which requires N_i, \mu_i \gtrsim 5 events per bin.

records.content:
Grouping continuous data into histogram bins discards information about where particles fell inside each bin. The Kolmogorov-Smirnov (K-S) test avoids binning entirely by comparing Cumulative Frequency Curves.

Empirical CDF (F_N(x)): Sort the N observed neutrino energies in ascending order. Plot the step-wise cumulative fraction of events from 0.0 to 1.0.

Theoretical CDF (F_0(x)): Integrate the continuous simulation density function to form its cumulative probability curve from 0.0 to 1.0.

K-S Statistic (D): Find the point along the energy axis x where the vertical distance between the two cumulative curves is largest:D = \sup_x |F_N(x) - F_0(x)|

Because D measures maximum vertical separation, it is sensitive purely to the shape of the distribution (e.g., shifts in energy scale or peak positions) without being biased by chosen histogram bin boundaries.

Once a test statistic t_{\text{obs}} (such as \chi^2_{\text{Pearson}} or D) is calculated from experimental data, we determine its p-value:p = P(t \ge t_{\text{obs}} \mid H_0) = \int_{t_{\text{obs}}}^\infty f(t \mid H_0) \, dt

In simple terms, the p-value is the area under the theoretical probability density curve f(t \mid H_0) from t_{\text{obs}} out to infinity.

records.content: Because neutrinos interact so weakly with matter, particle detectors often record very small numbers of events—sometimes just 0, 1, or 2 counts in high-energy histogram bins. In this low-statistics regime, the Gaussian assumption of Pearson’s \chi^2 fails, and we must construct fits using Poisson statistics.

hierarchy.lvl1: Statistical Methods for Neutrino Oscillation Parameter Estimation & Contour Generation
Statistical Methods for Neutrino Oscillation Parameter Estimation & Contour Generation

records.content:
The probability of observing exactly N_i discrete counts in bin i, when expecting a theoretical average rate of \mu_i(\mathbf{\psi}), is given by the standard Poisson probability mass function (PMF):P(N_i \mid \mu_i(\mathbf{\psi})) = \frac{\mu_i(\mathbf{\psi})^{N_i} e^{-\mu_i(\mathbf{\psi})}}{N_i!}

Assuming each histogram energy bin is statistically independent, the joint probability of observing an entire experimental dataset across all k bins is the product of their individual probabilities. This total joint probability is called the Likelihood function, \mathcal{L}(\mathbf{\psi}):\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{\psi}) = \prod_{i=1}^k \frac{\mu_i(\mathbf{\psi})^{N_i} e^{-\mu_i(\mathbf{\psi})}}{N_i!}

hierarchy.lvl1: Statistical Methods for Neutrino Oscillation Parameter Estimation & Contour Generation
Statistical Methods for Neutrino Oscillation Parameter Estimation & Contour Generation

records.content:
In practice, multiplying dozens of tiny probabilities together produces numbers extremely close to zero, causing computational rounding errors (underflow). Furthermore, differentiating products is algebraically difficult.

To solve this, we take the natural logarithm (\ln) of the likelihood function. Using logarithmic laws (\ln(ab) = \ln a + \ln b and \ln(a^b) = b \ln a), multiplication converts into simple addition:\ln \mathcal{L}(\mathbf{\psi}) = \sum_{i=1}^k \left[ N_i \ln \mu_i(\mathbf{\psi}) - \mu_i(\mathbf{\psi}) - \ln(N_i!) \right]

Because numerical optimization algorithms are designed to find the minimum of a function rather than its maximum, we multiply by -1 to define the Negative Log-Likelihood (NLL):-\ln \mathcal{L}(\mathbf{\psi}) = \sum_{i=1}^k \left[ \mu_i(\mathbf{\psi}) - N_i \ln \mu_i(\mathbf{\psi}) + \ln(N_i!) \right]

The trial parameters \mathbf{\psi} = (\sin^2 2\theta, \Delta m^2) that minimise the NLL represent the Maximum Likelihood Estimate (MLE)—the physics values that make our observed experimental data most probable.

hierarchy.lvl1: Statistical Methods for Neutrino Oscillation Parameter Estimation & Contour Generation
Statistical Methods for Neutrino Oscillation Parameter Estimation & Contour Generation

records.content:
While the NLL allows parameter estimation, its raw numerical value is not easily interpretable as a Goodness-of-Fit test because the term \sum \ln(N_i!) acts as an offset.

To construct a test statistic that behaves like a standard \chi^2, we form a Likelihood Ratio relative to the “saturated model”—an ideal, perfect hypothesis where the prediction in every bin matches the data exactly (\mu_i = N_i).

By defining \chi^2_{\text{Poisson}}(\mathbf{\psi}) \equiv 2 \left[ \ln \mathcal{L}(\text{perfect}) - \ln \mathcal{L}(\mathbf{\psi}) \right], the \ln(N_i!) terms cancel out completely, yielding the Baker-Cousins statistic:\chi^2_{\text{Poisson}}(\mathbf{\psi}) = 2 \sum_{i=1}^k \left[ \mu_i(\mathbf{\psi}) - N_i + N_i \ln \left(\frac{N_i}{\mu_i(\mathbf{\psi})}\right) \right]

Perfect Match: If predicted counts equal observed counts (\mu_i = N_i) in every bin, then \ln(1) = 0 and \mu_i - N_i = 0, giving \chi^2_{\text{Poisson}} = 0.

Zero-Count Bins: If a bin observes zero events (N_i = 0), the expression simplifies cleanly to 2 \mu_i(\mathbf{\psi}) using the limit \lim_{N_i \to 0} N_i \ln(N_i) = 0.

High-Statistics Limit: For large counts (N_i \gg 1), we can write \mu_i = N_i (1 + \delta) with \delta \ll 1. Applying the Taylor series expansion \ln(1 + \delta) \approx \delta - \frac{\delta^2}{2} demonstrates that \chi^2_{\text{Poisson}} converges exactly to Pearson’s \chi^2_{\text{Pearson}} = \sum \frac{(N_i - \mu_i)^2}{\mu_i}.

hierarchy.lvl1: Statistical Methods for Neutrino Oscillation Parameter Estimation & Contour Generation
Statistical Methods for Neutrino Oscillation Parameter Estimation & Contour Generation

records.content:
In an ideal A-level physics lab, every measurement error is purely random noise—repeating an experiment 10,000 times would make the average value converge perfectly to the true physical value (\sigma_{\bar{x}} = \sigma / \sqrt{N}).

In real-world particle physics, however, experiments are dominated by systematic uncertainties. These are non-random calibration offsets, flux uncertainties, or theoretical assumptions that shift your entire data distribution in a systematic way.

hierarchy.lvl1: Statistical Methods for Neutrino Oscillation Parameter Estimation & Contour Generation
Statistical Methods for Neutrino Oscillation Parameter Estimation & Contour Generation

records.content:
When extracting fundamental physics parameters of interest \mathbf{\psi} = (\sin^2 2\theta, \Delta m^2), our predictions also depend on auxiliary experimental parameters that we do not care about directly, but cannot ignore. We call these nuisance parameters, denoted \mathbf{\eta} = (\eta_1, \eta_2, \dots, \eta_m).

Typical examples in a neutrino experiment include:

Neutrino Flux Normalisation (\eta_{\text{flux}}): The overall intensity of the particle beam might be uncertain by \pm 5\%.

Detector Energy Scale (\eta_{\text{scale}}): The calibration factor converting light/charge hits into GeV might be off by \pm 2\%, shifting energy bins left or right.

Cross-Section Uncertainty (\eta_{\sigma}): Theoretical models predicting how neutrinos scatter off atomic nuclei carry uncertainties.

If a systematic parameter shifts away from its baseline value (\eta_j \neq \hat{\eta}_j), it modifies the expected event count in every bin \mu_i(\mathbf{\psi}, \mathbf{\eta}).

hierarchy.lvl1: Statistical Methods for Neutrino Oscillation Parameter Estimation & Contour Generation
Statistical Methods for Neutrino Oscillation Parameter Estimation & Contour Generation

records.content:
We rarely start an experiment completely ignorant of our apparatus. Prior calibration experiments (e.g., testing the detector in a beam line at CERN) constrain how far nuisance parameters are likely to deviate.

To incorporate this prior knowledge into our fit, we add a quadratic penalty term (also called a Gaussian constraint or prior) to the total test statistic:\chi^2_{\text{total}}(\mathbf{\psi}, \mathbf{\eta}) = \chi^2_{\text{data}}(\mathbf{\psi}, \mathbf{\eta}) + \sum_{j=1}^m \frac{(\eta_j - \hat{\eta}_j)^2}{\sigma_{\eta_j}^2}

Data Match Term (\chi^2_{\text{data}}): Measures how well the predicted spectrum matches the observed histogram (using the Poisson formula from Section 5).

Penalty Term (\sum \frac{(\eta_j - \hat{\eta}_j)^2}{\sigma_{\eta_j}^2}): Penalises the fit if it tries to pull systematic parameter \eta_j far away from its nominal central value \hat{\eta}_j, scaled by its external calibration uncertainty \sigma_{\eta_j}.

The Spring Analogy: Think of a penalty term like Hooke’s Law (E_p = \frac{1}{2} k x^2). The fitting routine is free to “stretch” a nuisance parameter to make the data fit better, but the spring pulls back with a quadratic restoring force. A shift of 1\sigma adds +1.0 to \chi^2_{\text{total}}, while a shift of 3\sigma adds a heavy penalty of +9.0.

When systematic parameters are correlated (e.g., shifting energy scale in one bin affects adjacent bins), the individual sum expands into a Covariance Matrix \mathbf{V}, yielding the full matrix penalty term:\chi^2_{\text{total}}(\mathbf{\psi}, \mathbf{\eta}) = \chi^2_{\text{data}}(\mathbf{\psi}, \mathbf{\eta}) + (\mathbf{\eta} - \hat{\mathbf{\eta}})^T \mathbf{V}^{-1} (\mathbf{\eta} - \hat{\mathbf{\eta}})

Our goal is to draw a 2D contour for physics parameters \mathbf{\psi}, but our total function \chi^2_{\text{total}}(\mathbf{\psi}, \mathbf{\eta}) lives in a high-dimensional space (often 2 physics parameters + 50 nuisance parameters!).

To reduce this complex space down to the physics parameters of interest, we use a technique called profiling:\chi^2_{\text{profile}}(\mathbf{\psi}) = \min_{\mathbf{\eta}} \chi^2_{\text{total}}(\mathbf{\psi}, \mathbf{\eta})

How Profiling Works Step-by-Step:

Fix the physics parameters to a specific grid point—say, \mathbf{\psi}_0 = (\sin^2 2\theta = 0.85, \Delta m^2 = 2.4 \times 10^{-3} \text{ eV}^2).

Hold \mathbf{\psi}_0 constant, and let an automated optimization algorithm adjust all m nuisance parameters \mathbf{\eta} simultaneously until it finds the combination \hat{\mathbf{\eta}}_{\text{best}} that minimises \chi^2_{\text{total}}.

Record that minimum value as \chi^2_{\text{profile}}(\mathbf{\psi}_0).

Repeat this minimisation for every point across the 2D physics grid.

Intuitive Visualization: Imagine looking at a 3D mountain range where height represents \chi^2, the x-axis is physics parameter \theta, and the y-axis is nuisance parameter \eta. Profiling means walking along the x-axis (\theta) and looking along the y-axis (\eta) to find the lowest valley point at each position. You project the floor of the valley onto a 2D curve, ensuring your physics measurements automatically absorb the worst-case impact of systematic uncertainties!

In experimental physics, single number estimates (e.g., \sin^2 2\theta = 0.86) are meaningless without an uncertainty boundary. We present our results as confidence regions (2D closed loops called contours) on a parameter grid of \Delta m^2 vs \sin^2 2\theta.

A 90\% Confidence Region means that if we were to repeat the exact same experiment 100 times under identical conditions, our constructed contour loops would enclose the true, fundamental physical parameter values in approximately 90 of those 100 trials.

In introductory statistics, a 1\sigma (68.3\%) confidence interval for a 1D Gaussian variable is found by moving outward from the minimum until the squared error increases by \Delta \chi^2 = z^2 = 1.0^2 = 1.0.

Wilks’ Theorem extends this simple idea to multi-dimensional fits. It states that if you have a large dataset, the test statistic:\Delta \chi^2(\mathbf{\psi}) = \chi^2_{\text{profile}}(\mathbf{\psi}) - \chi^2_{\text{profile}}(\hat{\mathbf{\psi}}_{\text{best}})

forms a multidimensional parabolic surface around the global best-fit point \hat{\mathbf{\psi}}_{\text{best}}.

To draw a contour boundary at a target Confidence Level (CL), we simply slice this 3D paraboloid at a constant height \Delta \chi^2_{\text{crit}}:

1D Fit (d=1, e.g., fitting only \theta):

68.27\% \text{ CL } (1\sigma): \Delta \chi^2 \le 1.00

90.00\% \text{ CL}: \Delta \chi^2 \le 2.71

95.45\% \text{ CL } (2\sigma): \Delta \chi^2 \le 3.84

2D Fit (d=2, fitting both \sin^2 2\theta and \Delta m^2):

68.27\% \text{ CL } (1\sigma): \Delta \chi^2 \le 2.30

90.00\% \text{ CL}: \Delta \chi^2 \le 4.61

95.45\% \text{ CL } (2\sigma): \Delta \chi^2 \le 6.18

The Topographic Map Analogy: Think of \Delta \chi^2(\mathbf{\psi}) as a bowl-shaped landscape where the global minimum is the deepest point at height zero. Drawing a 90\% allowed contour is like flooding the bowl with water up to a height of 4.61 units—the shoreline where water meets land defines your 90\% confidence boundary!

records.content:
Wilks’ theorem is an asymptotic approximation. It assumes the likelihood surface is a smooth, unbounded parabola. In neutrino oscillation searches, Wilks’ theorem fails for three physics reasons:

Physical Boundaries: Quantum mechanics restricts mixing angles to 0 \le \sin^2(2\theta) \le 1. If the true mixing angle is near maximum mixing (\sin^2 2\theta \approx 1.0), statistical noise cannot push the best-fit point above 1.0. This “wall” truncates the parabola, making standard \Delta \chi^2 cutoffs incorrect.

Non-linear Oscillations: Neutrino probabilities depend on \sin^2(1.27 \Delta m^2 L / E). Because of the sine-squared term, changing \Delta m^2 causes periodic, highly non-linear wiggles rather than a smooth parabola.

Low Event Counts: High-energy or appearance bins often contain zero or very few events, violating Gaussian normality.

Under these conditions, standard Wilks’ cutoffs lead to coverage problems—a nominal 90\% contour might actually only cover the true value 80\% of the time (under-coverage) or 98\% of the time (over-coverage).

records.content: To restore exact statistical coverage near physical boundaries or in low-statistics searches, Feldman and Cousins introduced a method that replaces fixed Wilks’ cutoffs (like 4.61) with custom critical values (\Delta \chi^2)_{\text{crit}}(\mathbf{\psi}_0) calculated specifically for every single point in physics parameter space.

records.content:
Define Observed Difference: At a specific grid point \mathbf{\psi}_0 = (\sin^2 2\theta_0, \Delta m^2_0), compute the observed profile test statistic relative to the physical global minimum:\Delta \chi^2_{\text{obs}}(\mathbf{\psi}_0) = \chi^2_{\text{profile}}(\mathbf{\psi}_0) - \chi^2_{\text{profile}}(\hat{\mathbf{\psi}}_{\text{best}})

Generate “Toy” Pseudo-Experiments (Monte Carlo Sampling):
Assuming \mathbf{\psi}_0 is the absolute truth, generate N_{\text{toy}} \approx 10,000 synthetic experimental datasets. For each bin i, sample a random integer from a Poisson distribution centered on the model prediction:N_{i, \text{toy}} \sim \text{Poisson}(\mu_i(\mathbf{\psi}_0, \hat{\mathbf{\eta}}_0))

Vary systematic nuisance parameters according to their Gaussian calibration uncertainties.

Fit Each Toy Dataset:
For each simulated toy dataset m:

Fit the toy data holding physics parameters fixed at \mathbf{\psi}_0 to find \chi^2_{\text{profile}, m}(\mathbf{\psi}_0).

Fit the toy data allowing physics parameters to float freely across the physical domain (0 \le \sin^2 2\theta \le 1) to find its own best-fit minimum \chi^2_{\text{profile}, m}(\hat{\mathbf{\psi}}_{\text{best}, m}).

Calculate the toy test statistic:\Delta \chi^2_m(\mathbf{\psi}_0) = \chi^2_{\text{profile}, m}(\mathbf{\psi}_0) - \chi^2_{\text{profile}, m}(\hat{\mathbf{\psi}}_{\text{best}, m})

Determine Custom Critical Cutoff:
Sort the 10,000 generated \Delta \chi^2_m(\mathbf{\psi}_0) values in ascending order. Find the 90\text{th} percentile value (the 9,000th entry). This value is the custom critical threshold, (\Delta \chi^2)_{\text{crit}}^{90\%}(\mathbf{\psi}_0).

Far from boundaries, (\Delta \chi^2)_{\text{crit}}^{90\%} \approx 4.61 (matching Wilks’ Theorem).

Near physical boundaries (\sin^2 2\theta \approx 1), (\Delta \chi^2)_{\text{crit}}^{90\%} can drop significantly (e.g., to 2.1 or 3.0).

Construct the Final Contour Boundary:
Compare the real experimental result \Delta \chi^2_{\text{obs}}(\mathbf{\psi}_0) against the custom cutoff (\Delta \chi^2)_{\text{crit}}^{90\%}(\mathbf{\psi}_0):\text{If } \Delta \chi^2_{\text{obs}}(\mathbf{\psi}_0) \le (\Delta \chi^2)_{\text{crit}}^{90\%}(\mathbf{\psi}_0) \implies \mathbf{\psi}_0 \text{ is ALLOWED at } 90\% \text{ CL}\text{If } \Delta \chi^2_{\text{obs}}(\mathbf{\psi}_0) > (\Delta \chi^2)_{\text{crit}}^{90\%}(\mathbf{\psi}_0) \implies \mathbf{\psi}_0 \text{ is EXCLUDED at } 90\% \text{ CL}

Repeating this decision rule for every point across the 2D grid traces out the exact boundary line of the allowed parameter region.
